cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized sequential word-RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph \(G\), terminates almost surely, always outputs a valid matching when it terminates, and outputs a maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\), with expected running time
\[(n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?\]
Here \(n=|V(G)|\), \(m=|E(G)|\), and the precise machine, input, probability and asymptotic conventions are below. In particular, the same program must meet every positive exponent slack; an algorithm chosen separately for each fixed slack is not the stated target.
cards.definitions:
Graph and optimum. Let \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge0}\), \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(E\) be a set of distinct unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, odd cycles, the empty graph and the edgeless graph are included. Put \(m=|E|\) and \(N=n+m+2\). A matching is a subset \(M\subseteq E\) such that no vertex belongs to two selected edges. Its cardinality is \(|M|\), and
\[\nu(G)=\max\{|M|:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}.\]
The empty matching is allowed, so this finite maximum exists on every input. The problem is unweighted. The algorithm must return the selected edges, not only the number \(\nu(G)\), a fractional solution, or a certificate that a perfect matching exists. Any maximum matching is acceptable.

Explicit representation. Use an edge list with headers \(n,m\), the vertex list \(1,\ldots,n\), and then \(m\) indexed pairs \((u_j,v_j)\) with \(1\le u_j<v_j\le n\) and no repeated pair. Edge indices are \(j=1,\ldots,m\); their order is arbitrary. Each integer occupies one machine word, so the entire input has \(2+n+2m\) words. Isolated vertices count in \(n\). The graph is a full list, not a succinct circuit or query oracle. The output consists of its cardinality \(t\) and a list of \(t\) distinct valid edge indices, in any order. Ordinary explicit adjacency lists can be converted to this form in \(O(n+m)\) word operations, preserving the target time scale. No guarantee is required on malformed inputs.

Machine. The algorithm fixes an integer \(b\ge2\) and, on inputs of size parameter \(N\), uses words of exactly
\[w=b\lceil\log_2N\rceil\]
bits. A word represents an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The machine has a fixed finite program, a constant number of word registers and random-access work memory addressed by one word, initially all zero. The input is read-only and the output is a sequential list of words. Each instruction operates on a constant number of words. Reading or writing an addressed word, copying, comparing, branching, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and arithmetic addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\) cost one operation. Integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor also cost one operation. A left or right shift by fewer than \(w\) positions discards bits outside the word and fills with zeros; a shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Larger exact integers use multiple words, and their processing is charged. A random instruction supplies one fresh uniform \(w\)-bit word, independent of all previous random words. There are no exact-real primitives, oracle calls, nonuniform advice, or precomputed tables supplied at no cost. The program may use \(w\) as the machine word length. Preprocessing, input access, initialization it performs and writing every output word are included in time.

Randomness and correctness. For a fixed valid input, the probability space is the infinite sequence of independent uniform random words used by the machine. Let \(T_A(G,R)\) count its operations, with value \(+\infty\) on a nonterminating execution. For every input, termination must have probability one. On every terminating execution, including those outside the success event, the output indices must represent a matching. On each input separately,
\[\Pr_R[\text{the output matching has cardinality }\nu(G)]\ge2/3.\]
The output may be suboptimal on other executions, but it must remain feasible. No distribution over input graphs is assumed, and success is not merely an expectation bound on matching size. A single program is used for every graph and edge-list order.

Almost-linear expected time. The expectation is over the algorithm's random words, with the input fixed. The notation in the question means that this same algorithm and word constant satisfy
\[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists C_\varepsilon>0\ \exists N_\varepsilon\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall G\text{ with }N\ge N_\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_R[T_A(G,R)]\le C_\varepsilon N^{1+\varepsilon}.\]
Constants and the threshold may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and on the fixed algorithm, but not on the graph, its density, its edge order or its random choices. The slack \(\varepsilon\) is not an input selecting a different program. This is a worst-case-over-inputs bound on expected time, not a bound on every individual random execution. The claim covers sparse and dense graphs simultaneously and allows subpolynomial overhead beyond polylogarithmic factors.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence statement or its logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a uniform finite program and a fixed word constant, prove almost-sure termination and feasibility on every terminating execution, prove per-input success probability at least \(2/3\), and establish the displayed expected-time bound for every positive exponent slack. All preprocessing, arithmetic and explicit output costs must fit that proof. A deterministic exact algorithm meeting the time bound is also a positive answer.

A negative answer must rule out all algorithms in the allowed randomized model. Equivalently, for every fixed word constant and program satisfying the termination, feasibility and success requirements, prove that there is some \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every size threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid graph encoding with \(N\ge N_0\) and \(\mathbb E[T_A]>C N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The exponent slack may depend on the program. A conditional running-time lower bound must name its unproved assumptions and does not alone establish this unconditional negation.

Algorithms only for bipartite graphs, a near-linear maximal matching, a fixed-accuracy approximation, the optimum size without an output matching, and average performance on random input graphs do not meet the full target. Bounds for pointer machines, parallel rounds, catalytic space or restricted algorithmic techniques must not be substituted for the permitted word-RAM expected time. No additive numerical tolerance applies to either exact optimality or the asymptotic exponent.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

importance.reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.

progress.text: Micali–Vazirani obtain the classical \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound, plus input reading for explicitly listed isolated vertices; later work supplies a full correctness theory.
Mucha–Sankowski construct maximum matchings using fast algebraic operations.
The authors of the Glauber-dynamics preprint acknowledge an incorrect coupling; its claimed almost-linear maximum-matching result does not hold.
Duan–Pettie–Su obtain linear-time approximation for each fixed accuracy parameter in general weighted graphs.
Chen and coauthors achieve almost-linear exact flow algorithms, giving the corresponding bipartite matching consequence.
Ansaripour–Danaei–Mehlhorn publish a detailed implementation and experimental study of Gabow’s general matching algorithm.
The catalytic-logspace revision constructs general maximum matchings with a polynomial-time bound, a different resource guarantee.

cards.status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No valid almost-linear exact general-graph algorithm was found in the bounded primary-source search. The June catalytic result gives a different polynomial-time/space guarantee; almost-linear flow applies to the bipartite consequence, and fixed-accuracy matching is weaker than exact optimality. The old Glauber-dynamics O(m log² n) claim is expressly invalidated by the authors in the current arXiv record. The retained target allows bounded-error randomization and expected word-RAM time; external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Classical exact algorithms use alternating paths to increase the size of a matching and blossoms to represent the odd-cycle structure of general graphs. Micali and Vazirani's 1980 algorithm has an \(O(m\sqrt n)\) RAM bound on its matching computation, or \(O(n+m\sqrt n)\) when reading all listed isolated vertices is included. Vazirani's later proof distinguishes this from an additional inverse-Ackermann factor in the pointer model. The historical bound is not evidence that such an overhead is necessary for every algorithm.

Bipartite maximum matching reduces to integral unit-capacity maximum flow with \(O(n+m)\) vertices and edges. Chen and coauthors explicitly obtain an almost-linear bipartite matching consequence from their exact flow theorem. Integrality in that setting yields an actual optimum matching. The reduction does not establish the same result on arbitrary undirected graphs, where no bipartition is available and odd-set constraints matter.

A triangle illustrates the integrality issue. Assigning value \(1/2\) to each edge respects a unit bound on the sum incident to every vertex, but has total value \(3/2\), whereas an integral matching has size at most one. For every odd vertex set \(S\), an integral matching contains at most \((|S|-1)/2\) edges entirely inside \(S\). These additional inequalities distinguish the general matching polytope from the simpler bipartite constraints.

Mucha and Sankowski construct maximum matchings by randomized algebraic computation in \(O(n^\omega)\) time for an available matrix-multiplication exponent \(\omega>2\); their Remark 1.1 records an extra logarithmic factor if the exponent is exactly two. Their finite-field arithmetic uses polynomially sized fields. This improves the classical bound on dense graphs, but even a quadratic-in-vertices bound does not approach the explicit input size on sparse graphs.

Duan, Pettie and Su prove a \((1-\delta)\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta^{-1}\log\delta^{-1})\) time, so the graph-processing time is linear for fixed \(\delta\). Unit edge weights give the cardinality case, with an additional \(O(n)\) cost for the explicit vertex list. Fixed positive relative error can still allow the loss of many matching edges as \(n\) grows. Making the allowed loss less than one when the optimum is proportional to \(n\) requires inverse-linear accuracy, for which that running-time expression is no longer almost linear.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

A 2011 preprint by Jindal, Kochar and Pal has an abstract claiming \(O(m\log^2 n)\) maximum matching via Glauber dynamics. Its current official arXiv record also contains the authors' correction: the coupling has incorrect marginals, so the mixing-time bound and the main result do not hold. The retained abstract must not be treated as a valid resolution of this target.

category_assignment.reason: The question asks for an almost-linear sequential algorithm for exact maximum-cardinality matching on static general graphs.

sentences: Maximum-cardinality matching selects as many pairwise vertex-disjoint edges as possible in an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph.
The target is one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that constructs an optimum matching with probability at least two thirds on every input.
It must halt almost surely, always return a valid matching when it halts, and have expected time within every fixed positive exponent slack above the full explicit input size.
A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm and all these guarantees or rule out every permitted randomized program with this expected-time behavior.
Known almost-linear bipartite algorithms, approximation schemes and catalytic-space results do not settle the general exact target, and the older Glauber-dynamics claim has an acknowledged error.

source_formulation.text: The inherited question asks for almost-linear exact maximum-cardinality matching on arbitrary explicitly represented simple undirected graphs. It already permits randomized success probability two thirds, expected running time, almost-sure termination and feasible output on every terminating run. These conventions are retained. The review specifies the word operations, graph/output encoding, isolated-vertex cost and same-program quantifier order. The 2024 implementation source distinguishes this general-graph frontier from the almost-linear bipartite consequence of flow algorithms.

quality_review.changes: Preserved importance 96 and the same-algorithm randomized expected almost-linear exact general matching target. Repaired malformed matching-size and constant-subscript expressions. Specified empty and disconnected graphs, isolated vertices, full indexed edge lists, exact output format, fixed logarithmic word length, unsigned arithmetic and shifts, initialized memory, independent random words and all computation costs. Made almost-sure termination, feasible failure outputs, per-input success and the full expected-time negation explicit in the Lean criterion. Rechecked algebraic, approximation, flow and catalytic frontiers and distinguished isolated-vertex input reading from O(m sqrt(n)) shorthand. Added the author-acknowledged invalidity of a matching O(m log² n) claim still visible in search abstracts.
checked_sources: Read Vazirani arXiv:2012.03582v1 full introduction, §1.2 and Theorem 8.6: O(m sqrt(n)) on RAM and extra inverse-Ackermann factor on pointer machines. Official INFORMS metadata confirms the renamed 2024 publication, online 7 May, Mathematics of Operations Research 49(3),2009–2047. Did not interpret the old-source frontier wording as independent evidence of current openness.

Read Mucha–Sankowski author-hosted FOCS 2004 full introduction, Remark 1.1 and §2.1. The construction is randomized, with O(n^omega) for an available exponent above two, a logarithmic extra factor at two and polynomial-size finite-field arithmetic. Confirmed original proceedings identity in the primary published PDF; did not replace it with the separate ESA planar result.

Read Duan–Pettie–Su arXiv:1112.0790v1 full introduction and Theorem 2 in §3.2. The general-graph bound is approximation with accuracy dependence; the exact weighted result in the same paper is bipartite. The retrieved PDF displays a November 2024 compilation date but the record is the December 2011 v1, so no new 2024 theorem was inferred.

Read Chen et al. arXiv:2203.00671v2 full abstract, Theorem 1.1, Corollary 1.2 and §1.1. Integral-capacity exact flow yields the explicitly stated bipartite matching consequence. The proof and numerical implementation were not rerun; a general-flow result was not conflated with general nonbipartite matching.

Read Ansaripour–Danaei–Mehlhorn arXiv:2409.14849v1 abstract, introduction and opening algorithm description; checked the experimental distinction between worst-case sparse families and random graphs. Their implementation discusses inverse-Ackermann union-find overhead. Experimental performance is not the card’s all-input guarantee.

Read Chakraborty et al. ECCC TR26-080 revision 1 full introduction, Theorems 1.1 and 4.3 and Definitions 2.1–2.2. The catalytic tape has arbitrary initial contents restored at termination, and CLP adds a polynomial-time bound. Revision date 1 June 2026 differs from manuscript date 31 May; official changelog simplifies Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.3 proofs. This is no almost-linear time theorem.

Bounded primary-source later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching valid general resolution. A search returned arXiv:1107.2482 with its old O(m log² n) claim; opened the current official v2 record and read the author comment explicitly invalidating the coupling, mixing bound and main result. This is an acknowledged error, not an uncertain accepted breakthrough. The erroneous proof was not treated as a theorem.

Checked all input encodings, empty and edgeless cases, output construction versus size, word-operation overflow, fixed word constant, probability-one termination, correctness versus expected output size, all edge-list orderings and the full same-program little-o quantifier order. Negative acceptance ranges over every permitted randomized expected-time program. No archive bodies were read and external proofs were not independently certified.
quality_review.scope: Checked target, definitions, quantifiers, answer criterion, context, significance and dated source claims. Bounded later-work checks do not independently certify every cited proof.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
